lead: Unit 3 connects microprocessor hardware to programs: how instructions are encoded, how operands are found, and how assembly code moves data, computes, branches and calls. After this unit you can read a small 8085, 8086 or 8051 program line by line, hand-assemble it, trace its flags and stack, and write loops, delays and look-up tables.
about: The unit starts with instruction formats and the functional classes of an instruction set (3.1), then shows how each operand is located by its addressing mode (3.2). The next four chapters turn that into programs: data transfer (3.3), arithmetic and logical operations with flags (3.4), branch, jump and call control flow (3.5), and stack plus subroutines (3.6). Chapter 3.7 puts these together in loops, cycle-counted delays and look-up tables. Chapter 3.8 shows the software tools that turn assembly source into machine code and run it on a simulator or board. Examples use 8085, 8086 and 8051, with PIC and ARM differences pointed to later units.

chapters.idea: An instruction is a coded command whose bit fields split into an opcode and operand or address parts, and instruction sets are grouped by what each instruction does.
chapters.depth: Cover the general instruction format: opcode field plus operand or address field. Compare zero-, one-, two- and three-address formats. Show 8085 1- to 3-byte instructions, 8086 variable 1- to 6-byte instructions, 8051 1- to 3-byte instructions and PIC 12/14-bit instruction words. Classify the set as data transfer, arithmetic, logical, branch/control, bit manipulation and machine control. Explain the assembly statement fields: label, mnemonic, operand and comment. Some syllabi call instruction format instruction encoding.

figure.aria: The instruction set tree has one root and five functional groups: data transfer, arithmetic, logical, branch, and bit/control.

chapters.example: Encode these two instructions and give the length in bytes: (a) 8085 MVI A, 3FH; (b) 8086 MOV AX, BX. Answer: (a) MVI A, 3FH is 3E 3F, 2 bytes: opcode 3E and immediate operand 3F. (b) MOV AX, BX is 89 D8, 2 bytes: opcode 89 and ModRM byte D8 where mod=11, reg=011 for BX and r/m=000 for AX.
chapters.trap: Do not treat every later byte as another opcode. In 8086 a later byte may be a ModRM byte or a displacement; instruction length is not fixed.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 stored-program concept and binary numbers; Unit 2 register names for 8085 and 8086.
chapters.leave: Detailed addressing modes to 3.2; flag meanings to 3.4; assembler directives to 3.8.

chapters.idea: An addressing mode is the rule that tells the CPU how to calculate the effective address of an operand.
chapters.depth: Define effective address. Cover implied or implicit, immediate, register, direct or absolute, register indirect, indexed, based, based-indexed, relative and stack modes. Map examples: 8085 MOV A,B (register), MVI A,32H (immediate), LDA 2050H (direct), MOV A,M (register indirect); 8086 [BX+SI+10H]; 8051 @R0 and MOVC A,@A+DPTR. Some syllabi call direct absolute and call register indirect simple indirect.

figure.aria: The addressing-mode tree lists implied, immediate, register, direct, indirect, indexed and relative modes under one root.

chapters.example: For 8086 with DS = 2000H, BX = 0100H, SI = 0020H and displacement 10H, find the effective address and physical address for MOV AL, [BX+SI+10H]. Answer: EA = 0100H + 0020H + 0010H = 0130H. Physical address = DS×10H + EA = 20000H + 0130H = 20130H. The byte is fetched from 20130H.
chapters.trap: In 8086 the effective address is not the physical address; add DS×10H. In 8085 a direct address such as LDA 2050H is already the physical address. [BX] defaults to DS, while [BP] defaults to SS.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 instruction fields; Unit 2 segment registers and memory organisation.
chapters.leave: Memory segmentation detail to Unit 2; ARM addressing modes to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Data transfer instructions copy a byte or word between registers, memory, I/O ports or the stack without doing arithmetic.
chapters.depth: Cover 8085 MOV, MVI, LDA, STA, LDAX, STAX, LHLD, SHLD, XCHG, IN and OUT; 8086 MOV, XCHG, LEA, LDS, LES, XLAT, IN and OUT; 8051 MOV, MOVX, MOVC, PUSH, POP, XCHD and SWAP. State that most transfers do not change flags. Mention that some syllabi group I/O instructions under data transfer.

figure.title: A, B and memory M
figure.aria: Three rows of three cells show register A, register B and memory M before, after MOV A,B, and after MOV M,A; the changed cell in each step is marked.

chapters.example: 8085 registers: A = 25H, B = 4AH, HL = 2050H, and memory [2050H] = FFH. Execute MOV A,B and then MOV M,A. Give A, B and [2050H]. Answer: MOV A,B copies B to A, so A = 4AH and B remains 4AH. MOV M,A writes A to memory at HL, so [2050H] = 4AH. Flags are unchanged.
chapters.trap: MOV A,B changes A only; it does not clear B. MOV M,r writes memory, while MOV r,M reads memory. PUSH and POP change SP, so they are not simple copies.
chapters.prereq: 3.2 addressing modes; Unit 2 registers and memory.
chapters.leave: Stack operation detail to 3.6; port hardware and interfacing to Unit 4 and Unit 5; string moves to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Arithmetic and logical instructions compute in the ALU and update flags that later branch instructions test.
chapters.depth: Cover 8085 ADD, ADC, SUB, SBB, INR, DCR, INX, DCX, DAD, CPI and CMP; 8086 MUL, IMUL, DIV and IDIV; DAA and DAS; AND, OR, XOR, CMA/NOT; rotates RLC, RRC, RAL and RAR; 8051 ADD, ADDC, SUBB, MUL, DIV and DA. Define flags Z, S, C, AC, P and OV. Mention bit-manipulation instructions as a related group.

figure.title: How an ALU instruction runs
figure.aria: A four-step flow: fetch operands, run the ALU operation, write the result, then update the flags register.

chapters.example: 8085: A = 9CH and B = 7FH. Execute ADD B. Find A and the flags C, AC, S, Z, P and OV. Answer: 9CH + 7FH = 11BH, so A = 1BH and carry C = 1. Low-nibble carry gives AC = 1. Result bit 7 is 0, so S = 0. Result is not zero, so Z = 0. 1BH has four 1 bits, so even parity gives P = 1. Signed values are -100 and +127, sum +27, so OV = 0.
chapters.trap: Carry and overflow are different: carry is unsigned, overflow is signed. In subtraction C = 1 means a borrow. INR and DCR do not affect C. DAA is used only after addition of BCD numbers.
chapters.leave: Multi-byte multiplication and division algorithms to advanced study; floating-point arithmetic to other subjects.

chapters.idea: Branch, jump and call instructions change the program counter; conditional ones decide from flags, and CALL also saves a return address.
chapters.depth: Cover unconditional JMP; conditional JZ, JNZ, JC, JNC, JP, JM, JPE and JPO; 8085 and 8086 forms; 8051 SJMP, AJMP, LJMP, JZ, JNZ, CJNE and DJNZ; CALL and RET; near and far calls; LOOP. Some syllabi call these control transfer instructions. Explain relative versus absolute targets.

figure.title: Conditional jump after CMP
figure.aria: CMP sets flags, then the Z flag decides whether the JZ path or the JNZ path is taken.

chapters.example: 8085: A = 05H, B = 07H. Execute CMP B, then JC LESS. State the flags and whether the jump is taken. Answer: CMP B computes 05H - 07H = FEH without changing A. A borrow is needed, so C = 1. The result is not zero, so Z = 0; bit 7 is 1, so S = 1. JC tests C = 1, so the jump to LESS is taken.
chapters.trap: CMP does not store the subtraction result; it only sets flags. For unsigned numbers, JC after CMP means A < B. CALL is not a jump: it pushes the address of the next instruction.
chapters.leave: Interrupts and interrupt vectors to Unit 4; ARM branch instructions to Unit 6; 8086 string repeat to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: The stack is last-in-first-out memory used for return addresses and saved data, and a subroutine is reusable code entered by CALL and left by RET.
chapters.depth: Cover stack pointer, PUSH and POP, CALL and RET, nested calls, parameter passing by registers, memory or stack, and stack overflow. Show 8085 and 8086 stack operation and 8051 stack use. Only a few universities teach re-entrant subroutines in detail; keep that short.

figure.title: Stack at 204EH, 204FH, 2050H
figure.aria: Stack bytes at 204EH, 204FH and 2050H: after CALL the return address is stored and SP points to 204EH; after RET the pointer returns to 2050H.

chapters.example: 8085: at address 2000H the instruction CALL 2100H is stored as 3 bytes. SP = 2050H. The subroutine at 2100H ends with RET. Show the stack bytes, SP and PC after CALL and after RET. Answer: after CALL, PC = 2100H, SP = 204EH, [204FH] = 20H and [204EH] = 03H, the return address 2003H. After RET, PC = 2003H and SP = 2050H.
chapters.trap: CALL pushes the address of the next instruction, not the address inside CALL. SP decrements before a write. In 8085, RET pops the low byte first, then the high byte.
chapters.prereq: 3.5 call and return; memory addressing from Unit 2.
chapters.leave: Interrupt-driven context saving to Unit 4; ARM stack and modes to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Assembly programs repeat work with counters and index registers, make delays by counting machine cycles, and read constants from look-up tables.
chapters.depth: Cover loop structure with counting and indexing, nested loops, delay calculation from T-states or machine cycles, and table access. Show 8085 delay loops and 8051 DJNZ. Cover look-up tables with LXI H and MOV A,M, with 8086 XLAT, or with 8051 MOVC A,@A+DPTR. Some syllabi call a delay a time delay loop.

figure.title: Delay loop
figure.aria: The loop loads count FFH, decrements C, tests for zero, and jumps back until C becomes zero.

chapters.example: Find the delay of this 8085 loop with a 3 MHz clock: MVI C,FFH; LOOP: DCR C; JNZ LOOP. Answer: MVI C,FFH takes 7 T. DCR C takes 4 T. JNZ takes 10 T when taken and 7 T when not taken. C goes from FFH to 00H, so DCR runs 255 times and JNZ is taken 254 times. Total T = 7 + 254×(4+10) + (4+7) = 3574 T. T-state time = 1/3 µs, so delay = 3574/3 µs = 1191.3 µs, about 1.19 ms.
chapters.trap: Count T-states, not just source lines. The last JNZ is not taken, so it uses 7 T, not 10 T. For 8051, one machine cycle uses 12 oscillator periods; do not mix clock frequency with machine-cycle rate.
chapters.prereq: 3.4 DCR and flags; 3.5 JNZ; Unit 2 timing and T-states.
chapters.leave: Hardware timers and counters to Unit 4; interrupt-based delays to Unit 4; embedded C timing to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: An assembler translates assembly source into machine code, a simulator runs that code without hardware, and an IDE joins editing, assembling, downloading and debugging into one tool.
chapters.depth: Cover assembler directives ORG, DB, DW, EQU and END; symbol table and location counter; object and hex files; linker; simulator and debugger; cross-assembler; IDE. Only a few universities teach assembler construction in detail; keep that part short. Mention that some syllabi call the whole set the development tool chain.

figure.title: Assembly tool chain
figure.aria: Assembly source goes through the assembler to an object or hex file, which is then run on a simulator or board.

chapters.example: Assemble this 8085 source and give the symbol table and bytes: ORG 2000H; START: MVI A,05H; LOOP: DCR A; JNZ LOOP; END. Answer: ORG sets the location counter to 2000H. MVI A,05H is 3E 05 at 2000H-2001H. DCR A is 3D at 2002H. JNZ LOOP is C2 02 20 at 2003H-2005H. Symbol table: START = 2000H, LOOP = 2002H. END produces no bytes.
chapters.trap: ORG sets the location counter but does not load memory by itself. Labels are addresses, not instructions. Directives such as EQU and END are not CPU instructions. The JNZ target is LOOP = 2002H, not 2003H.
chapters.leave: Embedded C compilation to Unit 4; linker and loader theory to advanced study.
